title: A Structured Unplugged Approach for Foundational AI Literacy in Primary Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of structured, concept-focused AI literacy instruction for primary school children. The authors argue that much existing AI education for young learners emphasizes using tools rather than understanding underlying concepts, which can leave children with misconceptions about how AI works, unrealistic expectations, and weak ability to recognize limitations, bias, and classification errors. The study asks whether a structured unplugged learning path can improve primary students’ understanding of foundational AI concepts, support related mathematical reasoning, and foster engagement.

The intervention is a structured four-module unplugged curriculum aligned with primary mathematics content and informed by constructivist, constructionist, and spiral-learning principles. Across four 2-hour modules, students were introduced to AI and computer science basics, classification principles, and multiple representations for classification such as Euler-Venn diagrams, tables, and decision trees. Activities included discussion of AI systems, a guided use of Code.org's AI for Oceans, monster and fish classification exercises, and embodied decision-tree tasks. The final module included a satisfaction questionnaire and a post-test with seven exercises assessing AI concepts and related mathematical reasoning.

The study was conducted with 31 fifth-grade students from two classes operating in an open-class model at one school in an anonymized country; the authors are based in Italy, but the participant country is not explicitly named. About 35% of students were female and 35% had special educational needs. The modules were delivered during curricular hours over four days by a university mathematics professor with extensive K-12 computer science education experience. Final analysis focused on 23 students who completed both the post-test and satisfaction questionnaire.

The paper concludes that the learning path was effective in supporting foundational AI literacy and related mathematical skills. Students showed improvement in AI terminology, classification reasoning, feature description, structured problem solving, and awareness of AI limitations. They also performed satisfactorily on frequency interpretation and set-based reasoning tasks. Engagement was high, and students particularly enjoyed interactive classification and real-world reasoning activities. However, the authors note challenges in abstraction, reasoning about implicit AI behaviors, and sustaining engagement in some repetitive tasks. They also acknowledge limitations in sample size, single-site scope, and lack of long-term follow-up, suggesting future work with larger and older student populations and stronger attention to representational scaffolding.

identified_tools.name: AI for Oceans
identified_tools.description: A Code.org educational activity that introduces basic AI and machine learning concepts through interactive model training and testing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within Module 1 as a hands-on machine-learning experience where primary students completed the first five steps to learn terms such as data, labels, model, and rule, and to observe how incorrect training leads to inaccurate recognition.

findings.finding_summary: Within a broader four-module AI literacy curriculum that included AI for Oceans as the only named AI tool, post-test results suggested improved AI concept understanding among fifth-grade students. The paper reports that in the AI Terms exercise, most students scored between 6 and 10 correct terms, and in the AI Scenarios exercise, 73.91% correctly recognized AI-related issues; however, results are not isolated to AI for Oceans alone. Engagement was also high, with qualitative feedback noting that students particularly enjoyed the AI for Oceans activity.
findings.measure: Post-test AI concept exercises (AI Terms, AI Scenarios) and qualitative engagement feedback

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General AI systems discussed as examples of everyday intelligent technologies, such as chatbots, voice assistants, recommender systems, and adaptive educational games.
identified_tools.use_case: Referenced in the motivation and background as examples of AI-powered systems children encounter, but not empirically evaluated as study interventions.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small empirical classroom study with 31 students overall and 23 completing the final assessment, using post-tests and satisfaction surveys but no control group or randomized comparison. Findings are promising but come from a single-site intervention with mainly descriptive outcome reporting.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive post-test percentages and student perceptions, but no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or pre/post causal estimates are provided. Impact appears encouraging yet remains unclear in magnitude.
